title: Public reckoning rolls on as IAG joins rush to cut ties with shamed KPMG
full_text:
IAG is dumping KPMG as its auditor, with the insurance giant announcing a tender process that explicitly excludes the underfire audit firm.
The decision to remove KPMG as its auditor, bringing an end to a 26-year relationship, comes after a torrid period for the big-four firm that has decimated its reputation amid a whistleblower scandal still reverberating through corporate Australia.
KPMG has been IAG’s auditor since the company’s ASX listing in 2000. The insurer’s chief executive, Nick Hawkins, and non-executive director JoAnne Stephenson, are both KPMG alumni.
“The board of Insurance Australia Group Limited (IAG) will begin a competitive tender process for the provision of external audit services,” IAG announced to the market on Friday.
“IAG has been well served by KPMG as external auditor since the company’s ASX listing in 2000, with a longstanding practice of regular lead audit partner rotation.” Putting tenure at the centre of its decision to move on from the beleaguered audit firm, IAG said KPMG would not be invited to participate in the tender process.
IAG will run the tender process during the current financial year, with shareholders asked to approve the appointment of the new audit firm once a decision has been made by the board.
IAG is the latest firm to walk away from KPMG amid a public reckoning over allegations the firm’s senior audit staff misused confidential client documents for their own gain.
The allegations were first aired by senator Deborah O’Neill in March this year and have claimed the scalps of its top executives including KPMG Australia chairman Martin Sheppard, chief executive Andrew Yates and chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett.
The claims included that audit partners had accessed documents, relied on inside information, and capitalised on director connections and compromised independence to win tenders, including at Macquarie and Westpac.
Banking behemoth Macquarie in August fired KPMG as its auditor, dumping the firm before it took over the role from incumbent PwC.
Lendlease also ditched KPMG in the wake of the scandal. Lendlease board papers were among the documents KPMG partners improperly accessed and used to win lucrative audit contracts.
The Macquarie audit was worth $74.9m to PwC in financial year 2025. KPMG earned $10.9m for the Lendlease audit in financial year 2026, and $11.6m from IAG.
A report prepared by Andrews Group and commissioned by KPMG, published on Thursday, made six cultural recommendations that were all supported by the firm’s senior management. It found KPMG took an “overly legalistic approach”, didn’t manage conflicts of interest, and failed to support the whistleblower by minimising their stand as a workplace grievance.
KPMG should review its stated values and identify the cultural drivers behind the failures; appoint an independent whistleblower protection officer; establish an in-house integrity office; conduct a full review of its whistleblower program; enhance its Ethics Champions Network; and advocate publicly for legislative reform to strengthen whistleblower protections. The whistleblower lost his job and told a parliamentary committee that “I would not do it again”.
